segments.text: Today's AI behaves differently from traditional software.
If you expect it to act like the software you're used to, its behavior can be confusing.
Two main differences help explain why.
First, AI learns patterns from examples, rather than relying only on instructions written
by programmers.
Second, it can work directly with unstructured data.
Think about how you interact with a standard application.
You're signing in to Spotify, but you type the wrong password.
Should the app open because you were close, or because your spelling was creative?
No.
You want it to follow an exact role.
Let me in only if the password matches.
Non-AI software operates entirely on instructions like this that people wrote.
A calculator follows strict steps for mathematical operations,
and a spreadsheet applies exact formulas to the information you enter.
This flowchart shows how those written rules look.
A user enters a password, and the system checks the input against a strict condition,
if the password matches.
From there, the path splits into absolute directions.
Following the green line, if the condition is met, the app opens.
Following the red line, if the input is anything else,
the app triggers an error message, asking you to try again.
The system does exactly what it is programmed to do.
Written rules return the same result every time.
So how does an artificial intelligence system generate answers
if no one wrote an exact rule for the task?
The difference is that AI learns patterns from examples during its training,
and uses those patterns to answer you.
People still write the code that trains and runs the AI,
but they don't write each answer.
This graphic uses a cooking analogy to break down the difference.
Rule-based software is like the cooking robot on the left, following a rigid recipe.
Someone wrote the steps.
The robot measures the ingredients, follows the instructions, and repeats the process.
Same recipe, same result every time.
Now look at the right side of the panel.
AI is like a chef who learned from preparing many different dishes.
The chef recognizes patterns, which ingredients work together,
how cooking methods affect food, and what substitutions might work.
The chef doesn't need a recipe.
By relying on internalized patterns, rather than strict recipes,
the system can adapt on the fly and output entirely new and different results.
This brings us to the second major difference, the shape of the data itself.
Traditional software usually needs information entered in a specific structure.
Think of a spreadsheet, organized neatly into distinct rows and columns.
That is structured data.
AI can work with unstructured data.
You don't need to organize your information into specific rows
and columns for the system to make sense of it.
This comparison shows the same short playlist in both formats.
On the left, traditional software uses structured data.
The table requires specific fields.
Blinding lights by the weekend is in the first play order position.
Levitating by Dua Lipa is second, and as it was by Harry Styles is third.
On the right, AI works with the unstructured version.
We have the exact same songs in artists,
but the information is communicated through messy handwritten notes,
scattered arrows saying start here, and crossed out text.
A traditional program, built to read a table,
would fail to process a scribble in the margins,
but an AI system can use this messy context to execute your intent.
The AI can interpret those notes because during training,
it learned patterns in handwriting, language, and visual clues
to understand what an arrow or a crossed out word implies.
But this flexibility comes with a trade-off.
Because the AI relies on interpreting broad patterns,
rather than checking a strict condition like a password,
its responses are harder to predict and inspect.
For instance, it might misread the visual cues and miss that crossed out song.
It might look great, but still have mistakes.
Recognizing how these systems operate tells us how to apply them.
Different jobs need different tools.
Choose the tool that fits the work.
